newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik fighters' thoughts more on war than on peace.
newsitem.headline: Tajik fighters' thoughts more on war than on peace.

text.p: Islamic guerrillas in war-torn Tajikistan, dismissing talk of plans for peace negotiations, said on Tuesday they were attacked by government tanks and helicopters the previous day.
"They attacked at six in the morning with tanks and helicopters," said opposition field commander Rakhmon Sanginov.

Embattled Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov and Islamic opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri agreed on Monday to meet on December 9 in northern Afghanistan, hoping to pave way for a lasting power-sharing deal to be signed in Moscow later.

Sanginov, speaking in his village of Tepa Samarkandi, 13 km (9 miles) east of the Tajik capital Dushanbe, said the fighting took place in hills above the village and its autumn-yellow orchards, the ridges frosted with the first snows of winter.
Dushanbe officials gave no word on the fighting but government military sources said one soldier had been killed and another wounded in an attack. Sanginov said his men had suffered no casualties.
Thousands of Russian troops in Dushanbe are helping prop up Rakhmonov's embattled government. They are on high alert after armed attacks on Russian soldiers in the city last week.
Opposition fighters are widely blamed for the attacks, which military and diplomatic sources say are being used to strengthen the opposition's hand before the talks in Afghanistan.
Children climbed over the wreck of a small van which villagers said was crushed by a government tank in the fighting. Tank tracks had chewed up part of the road.
Sanginov's men, shouldering machineguns and grenade launchers, crouched down behind a farm building as a Russian helicopter gunship buzzed around in circles in a clear blue sky.

"I don't believe negotiations with the government will amount to anything," said Sanginov, a large knife in his belt, a "Fly" anti-tank rocket strapped across his back and a black and gold scarf knotted around his throat.
"They'll gabble on and cheat us as they have in the past," he said.
Sanginov, a farm worker turned prominent field commmander, has lost two brothers and two daughters in the four-year-old civil war which has ripped the former Soviet republic apart.
The villagers of Tepa Samarkandi were busy on the land and appeared not to notice the helicopter.
"We're already used to it," said Matluba, a young woman in a turquoise scarf and a cotton dress printed with roses, as she watched over her children in the street outside her home.
Tens of thousands of people have lost their lives and many more have been displaced in the remote country which borders Afghanistan and China.

Diplomats say the opposition, which controls Tajikistan's mountainous eastern region, has improved as a fighting force and is applying mounting pressure on Rakhmonov as its guerrillas move slowly westwards towrds Dushanbe.
"If talks fail again the opposition could try and take the city (Dushanbe)," said one diplomat. "Their training has improved tremendously," he said.
